strengths: Introduces a large, professionally authored dataset of 992 articulated objects with 2,156 prismatic and 1,809 revolute joints, spanning 9 categories and 37 subcategories, which is a substantial resource for robot learning.
Provides not only isolated articulated assets but also six sim-ready indoor scenes, pixel-level part/affordance annotations, and modular interaction behaviors embedded in USD assets.
Adopts a clear top-down asset-authoring standard with detailed production guidelines, which improves consistency over datasets collected from heterogeneous 3D repositories.
Evaluates visual realism through multiple angles, including triangle-count comparisons, VGGT-based reconstruction quality, and CLIP feature-space alignment with real-world images.
Includes real-world physical validation using an optical motion capture system to compare simulated and real joint trajectories for selected objects such as drawers, microwaves, and ovens.

Demonstrates downstream utility via imitation learning experiments with ACT and Diffusion Policy, including real-only, sim-only, and real-sim-mixed settings, and a comparison against PartNet-Mobility on a microwave door-pulling task.
Provides extensive implementation details and hyperparameters in the appendix, and releases assets in USD with conversion pathways to URDF/MJCF, supporting practical adoption.
weaknesses: The physical-fidelity evaluation is narrow: only a few joint types/objects are validated with motion capture, yet the paper claims physical fidelity across the entire 992-asset dataset with thousands of joints. Broader sampling or systematic joint-level validation would be needed to support the central claim.

Visual-realism evaluation relies heavily on proxy metrics such as triangle count, CLIP t-SNE, and reconstruction with VGGT. These do not directly measure photorealism or robotic perceptual benefit, and the CLIP analysis could reflect rendering/domain differences rather than true visual fidelity.

The modular-interaction contribution is described but not rigorously evaluated. There is no ablation or user study showing that embedded behavior primitives are reusable, composable, or reduce development effort compared with code-based interaction implementations.

Downstream imitation-learning results show that sim-only policies transfer poorly compared with real-only training on several tasks, which weakens the claim that ArtVIP alone substantially reduces the sim-to-real gap. The mixed real+sim gains are expected and do not isolate the contribution of asset quality.
The PartNet-Mobility comparison is limited to one object category and one task. A broader digital-cousin or cross-dataset benchmark would be more convincing.

The reinforcement-learning experiment uses a single task (CloseTrashcan), and the reported Pearson correlation with real-world performance is difficult to verify from the main table because separate simulation and real-world success rates are not clearly presented.

The paper overclaims novelty in places, e.g., 'pioneers embedded modular interaction behaviors' and 'high physical fidelity,' without sufficient comparative or quantitative evidence across the dataset.

Reproducibility and release details are incomplete in the manuscript: the data link is blank, and there is no discussion of licensing, maintenance, annotation quality control, or inter-annotator agreement for the part labels.

Scaling is acknowledged as labor-intensive, but the paper does not quantify the trade-off between manual authoring cost and dataset utility, nor does it provide a feasible plan for community expansion beyond future generative methods.

strengths: Provides a substantial manually modeled articulated-object dataset: 992 objects, 9 categories, 37 subcategories, 2,156 prismatic and 1,809 revolute joints, plus six sim-ready indoor scenes and pixel-level affordance annotations.

Addresses a real gap in robot-learning assets: prior datasets such as PartNet-Mobility have weak visual/physical quality, while BEHAVIOR-1K is encrypted and simulator-locked; ArtVIP offers open USD assets with PBR-style materials and conversion guidance.
Includes useful production standards, collision/joint tuning procedures, modular interaction primitives, and detailed annotation labels that could benefit the community if released properly.

Demonstrates applicability through real-world and simulated imitation-learning experiments with ACT/DP, a PartNet-Mobility comparison, and an RL application with EAGLE, showing some practical relevance for sim-to-real manipulation.
weaknesses: Limited technical and algorithmic novelty: the main contribution is large-scale manual asset creation and packaging; the 'enhanced' joint drive equation is essentially gain scheduling/parameterization, and the modular behaviors are hand-authored primitives rather than a new method evaluated rigorously.

Visual-realism evaluation is not convincing: triangle count is a weak proxy for realism, CLIP t-SNE and VGGT reconstruction are qualitative/confounded, and there is no controlled perceptual study, rendering benchmark, or standard visual metric across datasets.

Physical-fidelity evaluation is too narrow: only a drawer force-displacement test and a few door mechanisms are quantitatively validated; there is no dataset-wide dynamics benchmark, no broad joint-trajectory comparison across categories, and insufficient statistical detail despite optical tracking being used.

Modular interaction is largely unevaluated: cross-asset effects, reusability, behavior correctness, and the claimed 394 assets/900+ joints are not tested or benchmarked, so the central interaction claim lacks empirical support.

Sim-to-real evidence is weaker than claimed: sim-only success rates are often low (e.g., 10–39%), indicating a persistent gap; real-sim-mixed gains are confounded by adding more data; real-only sometimes outperforms mixed settings; and the Table 2 ArtVIP-vs-PartNet-Mobility comparison may be confounded by asset/task selection.

Reproducibility and open-source claims are questionable: the abstract's data URL appears missing/placeholder, licensing and IP issues for digital twins of branded objects are not discussed, and conversion from USD to URDF/MJCF is not shown to preserve fidelity.

The dataset lacks standardized benchmark splits, evaluation protocols, and clear baselines for assessing asset quality; the paper does not provide a reproducible quantitative benchmark for future comparisons.

Presentation has clarity issues: several tables are misformatted or ambiguous (e.g., Table 2 real-only row, Table 3 sim/real split), key physical-fidelity details are deferred, and the Pearson correlation calculation is difficult to verify from the main table.

strengths: Introduces a large-scale, open-source articulated object dataset (992 assets, 9 categories, 37 subcategories) with digital-twin quality, USD format, scene assets, and annotations, addressing a real bottleneck in robot learning.

Provides detailed asset creation methodology and unified standards, including hierarchical assembly (assembly/module/mesh), collision modeling, joint tuning, modular interaction primitives, and pixel-level affordance labels.

Offers broad empirical validation: visual realism comparison (triangle count, VGGT reconstruction, CLIP/t-SNE), physical fidelity via optical motion capture, imitation learning with ACT/DP across real-only/sim-only/mixed settings, and RL with EAGLE plus sim-to-real correlation.

Demonstrates practical utility: mixing ArtVIP simulation data with real data improves success rates across four manipulation tasks, and comparisons to PartNet-Mobility show better zero-shot and mixed-data transfer for microwave door pulling.

Strong reproducibility and community value: fully open-source assets, production guidelines, compatibility with Isaac Sim/USD and conversion to URDF/MJCF, six sim-ready scenes, and modular embedded interactions.
weaknesses: Visual realism evaluation relies primarily on proxy metrics (triangle count, VGGT reconstruction, CLIP feature t-SNE) rather than a rigorous perceptual study or a broad set of downstream visual tasks; CLIP/t-SNE comparisons can be sensitive to sampling and rendering choices.

Physical fidelity is quantitatively validated on only a few object types (drawer, microwave door, oven door), so the claim of general physical fidelity across 992 assets and diverse joint types is not fully established.

Modular interaction behaviors are a key novelty but are not systematically evaluated for correctness, coverage, or usability; the paper reports counts but lacks quantitative task-level benchmarks isolating the benefit of embedded interaction semantics.

Sim-only imitation learning success rates are relatively low (e.g., ACT 12% OpenCabinet, 13% SlideShelf; DP 10% OpenCabinet), suggesting a persistent sim-to-real gap; mixed-data gains are convincing but the high-fidelity zero-shot claim is somewhat overstated.

Comparisons with prior datasets are not uniformly comprehensive: PartNet-Mobility is compared on selected categories and one real-world task, while BEHAVIOR-1K comparison is mostly qualitative/rendering-based and constrained by its encrypted access.

The paper could better report per-category or per-joint-type physical parameter tuning accuracy, failure cases, and asset quality statistics; the manual-labor bottleneck is acknowledged but not quantified in terms of coverage limitations.
